opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. With PixelRush, the core problem we wanted to tackle is that diffusion models are trained at a fixed resolution, usually around 1024 by 1024. If you simply ask them to generate at much higher resolution, you get artifacts: repeated objects, duplicated faces, broken global structure. On top of that, the compute cost grows quickly with the number of pixels, which matters a lot to us at Qualcomm because we care about running these models efficiently, ideally on the device.

Many existing approaches to high-resolution generation are training-free, which is nice, but they tend to be slow. They often run a full multi-step diffusion process at low resolution, upscale, and then run another long denoising process at high resolution, sometimes with overlapping patches that are each denoised many times. That can take minutes per image.

Our approach keeps the tuning-free spirit, so we don't retrain the base model, but we rethink the pipeline for speed. First we generate a good low-resolution image that captures the global layout and semantics. Then we move to the higher resolution and work patch by patch, but instead of starting each patch from pure noise and running the whole trajectory, we inject only a partial amount of noise and denoise from an intermediate point. The low-resolution result already gives you structure, so the high-resolution stage mainly has to add fine detail and texture. That lets us use very few denoising steps and works well with the newer few-step distilled models.

There are a couple of practical details that make a big difference. One is how you blend patches. If you naively stitch them you see seams, and if you average overlaps too aggressively you get blur. So we pay attention to how overlapping regions are combined so detail is preserved without visible boundaries. Another is noise handling. When you denoise with very few steps, the noise level and the statistics of the injected noise matter much more, and getting that wrong produces oversmoothed or overly noisy textures. So we adjust the noise injection to keep fine detail sharp.

The result is that we can generate high-resolution images, up to 4K and beyond, with quality competitive with the slower training-free methods, but significantly faster, closer to seconds instead of minutes. For us, the bigger picture is that high-resolution generative AI shouldn't require a data center for every image. If you design the pipeline carefully, you can get very high quality at a fraction of the compute.

r001.rationale: The response describes moving to higher resolution but does not say whether upsampling occurs in RGB pixel space or latent space.

r002.rationale: It says the high-resolution stage works patch by patch, but does not state that patches partition the latent representation or that this limits memory use.

r003.rationale: It warns that naively stitching patches can create visible seams.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, great to be here. So the core idea behind PixelRush is pretty simple to state: high-resolution generation shouldn't cost you quadratically more compute just because you want more pixels. Most diffusion and flow-based models operate in a latent space, and then you have a decoder that upsamples, but when you push to 2K, 4K, or beyond, either the latent grid grows and attention becomes the bottleneck, or you tile, and then you fight seams and global coherence.

What we do instead is decouple the problem into two stages that are trained to cooperate. The first stage handles the global structure: composition, layout, lighting, the semantic content of the scene. That runs at a modest resolution where attention is cheap and the model can reason about the whole image at once. The second stage is a hierarchical refinement that adds detail in a coarse-to-fine manner, but the key is that it's conditioned on the first stage's features, not just on the pixels. So it's not a naive super-resolution bolt-on. The refinement network knows what the object is supposed to be, so when it hallucinates texture on a fabric or edges on a building, those details are consistent with the semantics.

The second piece is efficiency in the refinement itself. Rather than denoising at full resolution for many steps, we use a very small number of steps at the high-resolution levels, because most of the hard decisions have already been made at low resolution. Structure is expensive to get right; texture is comparatively local and can be handled with local or windowed operations. So we push almost all of the global attention down to the cheap stage and keep the expensive stage as local as possible. That's where the "rush" comes from. In practice we see on the order of several-fold speedups over running a full-resolution diffusion process, with better detail fidelity than tiling approaches.

And then there's the training side, which I think people underestimate. If you train the refinement stage only on clean low-res features, it never learns to correct the mistakes the first stage actually makes. So we train with the real outputs of stage one, including its imperfections, so the refinement learns to be robust and to fix, not just to upsample. That mismatch between training and inference is, in my experience, one of the biggest reasons cascaded systems fall apart.

One more thing I'd add, because it comes up a lot: we care about on-device feasibility, not just server throughput. Memory, not FLOPs, is often the hard constraint on a phone. So the hierarchical design also means you never hold a full high-resolution activation map for the global model, which is what makes something like this plausible on mobile hardware rather than just a data-center demo.

r001.rationale: The response discusses latent-space models and refinement, but does not state that PixelRush upsamples in RGB pixel space.

r002.rationale: It mentions tiling and local or windowed operations, but does not say PixelRush partitions the latent representation into manageable patches to limit memory use.

r003.rationale: It says tiling can lead to seams and global-coherence problems, communicating that separately tiled image regions can produce visible seams.

astra-6.text:
The key is to separate the amount of detail you want in the output from the amount of computation you need to establish the overall structure. At high resolution, processing every pixel equally at every step becomes very expensive. But the composition and the fine texture don’t necessarily need the same treatment.

So I would frame the approach as getting the global structure right efficiently, then spending computation where it improves the detail. The challenge is preserving consistency across the image as you do that. You want higher resolution to give you meaningful detail, rather than simply a larger image or sharper-looking artifacts.

r001.rationale: The response discusses high-resolution computation but does not say PixelRush upsamples in RGB pixel space rather than latent space.

r002.rationale: It does not mention partitioning the latent representation into patches to limit memory use.

r003.rationale: It mentions preserving consistency, but does not warn that separately created image patches can produce visible seams.

sol-6.1.text: The key is to separate getting the overall structure right from generating the fine detail. If you try to do everything at full resolution from the beginning, the computation becomes very expensive. So we approach it progressively: establish the global composition at a lower resolution, then introduce higher-resolution detail as generation proceeds. The challenge is maintaining consistency—you want those details to belong to the same image, rather than looking like independently generated patches. That balance between global coherence, local detail, and computational cost is central to the approach.

r002.rationale: It does not state that PixelRush partitions the latent representation into patches to limit memory use.

r003.rationale: It mentions consistency between details and the overall image, but does not warn that separately creating image patches can produce visible seams.
